content: The Xpert cartridges and reagents typically require storage at temperatures between 2°C and 28°C. The Xpert analyzer device must be operated in a laboratory environment with a temperature range of 15°C to 30°C, a stable and continuous electricity supply, no direct sunlight, and minimal dust and humidity. Point-of-care (POC) assays necessitate specific training for the device being used, although prior laboratory experience is not mandatory. Assays should be transported under conditions similar to their storage requirements and disposed of using appropriate waste management procedures to prevent the release of harmful chemicals into the environment. For example, Xpert cartridges require high-temperature incineration for disposal. A feasibility study, known as the CT2 Study, was conducted in Yangon, Myanmar, to evaluate a decentralized, community-based test-and-treat model for hepatitis C virus (HCV) care. This model utilized POC testing for HCV diagnosis, including the Abbott® SD Bioline HCV rapid antibody test and the Cepheid® GeneXpert® POC HCV Viral Load assay. General practitioners led the care process, prescribing pangenotypic generic direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) to eligible participants. The study was conducted at two sites: one for individuals who inject drugs and another for those with liver disease. Both sites provided on-site testing and treatment services in a one-stop shop model. Between January 2019 and August 2020, 633 participants were recruited, 606 underwent HCV viral load testing, and 488 initiated DAA treatment for active HCV infection. Of these, 477 (98%) completed therapy, and 421 (92%) achieved sustained virological response at 12 weeks (SVR12). Although the study used the GeneXpert device, the principles and lessons learned are applicable to other POC devices. Key operational considerations for implementing POC HCV testing in community settings included training, laboratory setup, and quality control. Laboratory technicians, nurses, and general practitioners received training in three stages: initial orientation, on-site practical training after device installation, and training for participation in an external quality assessment scheme (EQAS). Laboratory technicians were primarily responsible for phlebotomy and operating the device. They found the staggered training sessions helpful for addressing questions as they became more familiar with the device. Nurses and general practitioners were also trained to perform tests but did not maintain competency due to infrequent use of the device. Overall, staff reported that the GeneXpert analyzer was simple and easy to operate but sensitive to errors during specimen preparation, particularly when handling venous blood plasma specimens. The study was conducted in two community-based clinics, with rooms renovated to provide laboratory services. Each laboratory was equipped with a four-module GeneXpert machine, an online uninterruptible power supply (UPS), a laptop, a barcode scanner, a printer, a centrifuge, an air conditioner, and other necessary infrastructure. One site underwent additional renovations to improve conditions for the GeneXpert machine, such as reducing dust and humidity and limiting room access. The facilities relied on small on-site generators for power backup, which required manual startup during outages. Unstable electricity supply, particularly during the rainy season, caused recurring errors with the GeneXpert machine. Temperature and humidity control posed challenges for test kit and reagent storage. Daily temperatures in Yangon ranged from 17°C to 39°C, with humidity levels between 65% and 85%. Test kits and reagents required storage below 30°C and were vulnerable to damage from high humidity. Sites were advised to store kits in refrigerators before use, but this required substantial space. Standard household refrigerators were used, though laboratory-grade refrigerators may be better suited for stock storage and monitoring. GeneXpert devices required annual maintenance, including on-site checks by technical support personnel, as well as ad hoc maintenance and module replacements for recurrent errors. Across the study, the error rate for the GeneXpert HCV Viral Load assay was 5% of the total tests conducted. Errors were defined as any erroneous output, no result, or invalid result. Minimal internal quality control (IQC) was performed midway through the study, involving weekly unblinded testing with known positive and negative specimens. Xpert HCV Viral Load cartridges had a shelf life of 12 months from manufacture, but this was reduced to 6–9 months after clearing customs and arriving at clinics. Regular supply via local distributors and accurate demand forecasting were essential. Confirmation of undetectable HCV RNA in previously viremic individuals is critical for assessing virological response to DAA treatment. A single negative HCV RNA test at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12) is now the benchmark for assessing treatment outcomes and cure. Laboratory-based nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA remains the gold standard, but POC HCV RNA NAT assays with comparable sensitivity are recommended as an alternative for testing in remote settings. The limit of detection (LoD) for GeneXpert using venous blood is 10 IU/mL, while for fingerstick blood, it is 100 IU/mL. These assays are acceptable for diagnosing viremic HCV infection, but further studies are needed to establish their use as a test of cure. Reflex testing, which links HCV RNA testing to a positive HCV antibody result, is recommended to improve linkage to care and treatment. This can be implemented through laboratory-based or clinic-based reflex testing. Laboratory-based reflex testing uses the same or duplicate specimen for HCV RNA testing after a positive antibody result. Clinic-based reflex testing involves immediate specimen collection for HCV RNA testing following a positive rapid diagnostic antibody test. Reflex testing reduces turnaround time, increases linkage to care, and eliminates the need for additional clinic visits. In summary, while laboratory-based NAT assays remain the standard for HCV diagnosis and monitoring, POC assays and reflex testing strategies offer practical alternatives to improve access to care, particularly in resource-limited settings. Further research is needed to optimize these approaches and address gaps in data for specific populations.
